extracted.intended_audience: scholars and educated readers interested in classics, political communication, and the history of public opinion
extracted.subtask_description: An expository essay comparing ancient and modern organs of public opinion, showing how genres (epic, lyric, drama) and institutions (assembly, theatre, press) enable or limit the formation and exercise of collective sentiment. It traces the features that made certain media influential in different historical settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper press as 'double power' (ubiquitous instructor + rapid interpreter)
rubrics_metrics.description: The newspaper press wields a double power, 'at once as the ubiquitous instructor and as the rapid interpreter of a national mind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the Gordon episode: a popular biography and newspaper coverage in a few weeks made broad facts of his career widely known and could have concentrated public opinion rapidly enough to threaten a Ministry. Emphasises speed, reach, and the ability to crystallize feeling into political force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional/personal biography + press can concentrate popular imagination quickly
rubrics_metrics.description: A short popular biography plus newspaper discussion can make the broad facts of a person's career known nationwide and rapidly concentrate public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: General Gordon — weeks of coverage produced a national fixation; consequence: immediate political effects (rumour of his death could topple a Ministry). Shows the modern press's unique capacity to create focused public sentiment around individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of a political assembly (audience with agency) as a condition for media influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Media have greater political influence where an active popular assembly exists, because hearers are also voters/decision-makers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Athenian dramatists addressed audiences who were, constitutionally, members of the assembly and might act on sentiment the next day. Contrast with epic poets, whose audiences lacked such practical agency. Thus institutional context (assembly, courts) amplifies a medium's capacity to affect policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic performance as a vehicle for political and moral persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy and drama could be used by skilful authors to inculcate views, to urge or oppose particular measures, and to function like party journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aeschylus in the Furies advocates a political stance (e.g., supporting claims in the Troad, protesting reforms). Euripides contains unmistakable allusions to contemporary wars/politics (Heracleidae, Supplices). Voltaire's tragedies similarly insinuated popular opinions in eras without modern journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Chorus as a visible link between theatre and public sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus functions as a lineal descendant of the Homeric 'Tis', constituting a visible link between audience and drama and bringing the average spectator into sympathy with the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Its interest is less in maxims uttered than in its role in connecting the audience to the play, thereby predisposing spectators to seize any contemporary or political significance in the drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre suitability: epic vs lyric vs drama for expressing/affecting public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic narratives express mass belief and feeling in ages without direct organs of utterance; lyric poetry expresses the individual poet's voice; drama addresses a politically active community and can therefore influence action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homeric epic reflected an undertone of popular comment but lacked institutional mechanism for political effect; lyric poets (Tyrtaeus, Sappho, Pindar) express personal opinion; drama (Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides) speaks to audiences who can translate sentiment into civic action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homeric 'Tis' as the prototype of popular-speaking sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: The Homeric indefinite pronoun 'Tis' represents the average man and functions as the mouthpiece of popular sentiment: 'Thus would a man speak, with a glance at his neighbor.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tis appears at critical moments to express what common opinion would say (approval, blame, gossip). Examples include reactions during the fight over Patroclus' corpse, Hector's imagined response, and social commentary in the Odyssey. Tis can be generous or ignoble (e.g., gloating over Hector's corpse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-audience traits that make popular commentary effective: quick perception and readiness of speech
rubrics_metrics.description: The Homeric Greek's quickness of perception and readiness of speech fuelled an alert social public opinion—attributes that allow popular commentary to arise spontaneously and be influential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These cultural-psychological qualities explain why an undertone of popular comment pervades Homeric poems; they make the representative 'Tis' vibrant, immediate, and capable of shaping social attitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion's moral mechanisms: aidos (shame/reverence) vs nemesis (inner moral sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public opinion operates via conventions like aidos (reverence/shame relative to communal standards) and interacts with nemesis (the individual's inner moral sense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aidos is relative to the collective sayings of 'Tis' and can be conventional or low; nemesis is obedience to an inner moral voice. Their interplay can recommend the same conduct (harmonious) or conflict (e.g., taking rank over merit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of opinion insufficient without courage/power to act
rubrics_metrics.description: Public opinion may exist and be articulated, but if it lacks the power or courage to act, it will not bring practical change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Telemachus's appeal to the men of Ithaca to stop the suitors invoked nemesis and aidos but failed—the public opinion existed but had not the courage to act. Highlights the difference between sentiment and enforceable political will.
